title: Adoration of Child (Tondo: Holy Family and Baptist)
description:
An oil and wood painting depicting the Holy Family and John the Baptist. The Virgin Mary, Saint Joseph, and John sit around baby Jesus and gaze down at him. Jesus stares outward at the viewer, meeting our gaze.
The Virgin Mary is centered in the composition, wearing her blue and green mantle and a red tunic. Her head is partially covered in a wrap. A halo is faintly seen above her head. She is on her knees, leaning over baby Jesus, her hands in prayer.
In the middleground, to the viewer's right, sits Saint Joseph. His beard is clean and neatly trimmed into two points. He, like Mary, is dressed in a red tunic. A light brown mantle is laid over his lap. A faint halo is seen above his head. He rests his chin in his hands as he looks towards the baby Jesus.
To the right of Mary (the viewer's left), a baby John the Baptist leans over Jesus. He is dressed in a more muted blue than Mary; his mantle is held closed by a red strip of fabric tied around his waist. Visible over his head of curly hair is a halo.
Between John and Mary, laying on the floor, is baby Jesus. He lays on a dark blue pillow or mat. A shawl, nearly transparent, is draped over his waist and around his shoulder. He clutches the end in his right fist. A halo is seen above his head.

title: Portrait of Plato
description:
An oil on canvas depicting Plato. Plato is centered in the composition, seemingly emerging from the dark background: he is starkly lit in an otherwise dark composition, his face depicted in chiaroscuro.. His brow is furrorwed and his philosopher's coat (a patchwork tribon) falls off of his right shoulder. He looks intently at the viewer, guesturing towards a mirror with his left hand. The mirror, which he holds with his right hand, is set on a table.
On the table is inscribed: "LA PIV' GRAN VITORIA/ CHE POSSA HAVERE/ VN HVOMO E'VINCERE/ SE' STESSO." This is a passage from Plato's "Laws."

title: Lunette of Saint Anna, the Virgin and 2 Monks
description:
A Ceramic Lunette, which is rendered in 8 parts. The central image shows the Madonna and child. Behind Mary, with a hand on her shoulders is St. Anne; they are positioned to appear as if Mary is Sitting on Anne's lap with the infant Christ subsequently sitting in hers. Two Male saints kneel, one on each side, with their heads bowed toward the infant Christ. The three saints are haloed, thought the Virgin and Child are not, presumably because the are suspended too far forward in relief and would block the other figures. Around the top of the arch a Mask is presented at the crown of the arch, sculpted greenery and fruits then fall down either side of the arch.
Saint Anne is identified in her hagiography as the mother of the Virgin Mary. This explains her positioning with this pointedly young-looking depiction of the Virgin. Mary wears blue, so she stands out completely against the white glaze finish of her mother, the other two saints, and the Baby in her lap. The three older saints in turn stand out against the blue background, with Saint Anne acting as a sort of border around the Virgin.
The male saint on the right side of the image (when viewing) is St. Dominic. He holds a cross, Lilies and a book (there is also a scull nestled in the crook of his arm, though this is less typical of his attributes). He is dressed in robes and has his hair cut into a tonsure but is clean shaven.
The Second male saint, on the left side, is St. Augustine of Hippo. He holds a book against his knee. The symbol of a book is very common among saints, but is an attribute of Augustine. In his other hand he holds what appears to be a flaming heart, which would be a more identifiable symbols of Augustine.

title: Roman Vestal
description:
A bust of a Roman Vestal. She is depicted from the chest up, and her head is hooded with thin cloth that drapes to her shoulders, joining the fabric of her dress or tunic. Her hair is visible laying flat and unbound beneath the cloak, though her bangs are styled back away from her face. Her features are soft and she casts her eyes downward.
The Vestals (Also called Vestal Virgins), were a group of priestesses of the Roman goddess Vesta. Vesta is goddess of the hearth, home and family, more often represented herself as a sacred flame than in human form (Her Greek equivalent is Hestia). The Vestals who oversaw her sacred temples were selected before puberty and took vows to the goddess, which lasted 30 years. During this period they were expected to stay virgins, and breaking their vow of chastity was met with either burning or entombment. In addition to the vows of Chastity, Vestals pledged their service to the goddess, learning and performing rites which were thought to maintain the Roman State.
In exchange they were the only ones allowed to enter the temples of Vesta, which they did to maintain the sacred fire in her hearth, and they were granted privileges above those of all other women in the empire, including those women in the royal family. Rights of the Vestals included: The ability to use a carpentum, a two-wheeled horse drawn carriage not dissimilar to those ridden by triumphant generals in processions; right away, with the impeding a Vestal's passing being punishable by death; access to and ring-side seating at public games including gladiatorial fights and plays.
Additionally a Vesta could pardon any condemned person who was en route to execution, simply by touching them, so long as the meeting had not been pre-arranged.

title: Venus of Cyrene
description:
A statue of a Venus, presented in the Nude standing contrapposto. She is missing her head and arms, but otherwise is very in tact. If the image was fully in tact, it would have presented a young goddess emerging from the water, Right hand lowered to cover herself, and left hand reaching to pick up the cloth; At the right hip of the Venus the image of a hydra with a fish in it's mouth is coiled on it's front with drapery hanging from the tail of the creature (presumably the dress of the Venus herself).
This image is a recreation of the Venus of Cyrene, which was excavated in 1913. The original was dated to approximately 130 A.C. and was itself a copy of the Venus Cnidia by Praxiteles, (known only through Roman copies). Praxiteles is accredited with the first depiction of a female nude in the cannon of Greek works of art.
In 2002 the Venus of Cyrene was transferred from the Minister of Cultural Heritage and Activities in Italy to the Libyan Republic in a repatriation that was surrounded in criticism. The deal was finalized in 2008 and the work was sent to a small museum with minimal security. As Libya descended into revolution in 2011, artifacts from Cyrene were targeted, located and sold on the black market or destroyed my militant groups moving through the area. The exact fate of the Venus is not known, but it was confirmed to have disappeared from the museum housing it. Sometimes referred to as the "Lost Venus" it can be viewed in the form of a plaster mold taken in the 1930s, but the fate of the original is not known.

title: Della Robbia Style Angel
description:
Ceramic disk showing the image of a cherub. The head, shoulders and wings of the angel are visible in the center of the disk. He is glazed white and haloed so that the cherub stands out against the blue field behind him. Around the exterior of the disk a relief of grapes, lemons and leaves is painted in bright colors.
The relief in the collection is probably modern though reminiscent of relief works in the style of Andrea Della Robbia. The Della Robbia style is identified by the bright colored glazes (Traditionally applied over terra cotta so that the color soaked in to the clay), mostly in combinations of blues and whites. The material beneath the glaze on this image is not known, but holds the typical colors of the style which the piece is trying to emulate.

title: Louis XIII Style Side Table
description: A Louis XIII Style Side Table from Spain. The style is characterized by geometric forms and turned wood moldings, usually finished with varnish. This table is characteristic with straight lines, except on the legs, which are turned wood to show a pattern of stacked orbs. The side facing away from the couch has a drawer with a metal pull tab. It is finished with a dark varnish. The legs are joined with cross beams across each outer edge at the bottom.

title: (1 of 2) French Walnut Armchair
description:
One of two walnut armchairs. The set are constructed of sturdy wood and feature draping foliage carved into the arms both at the front of the chair and where the arm connects to the backing. The legs are turned wood, and the feet are carved to sit with wide unfurling curves akin to a flower turned up-side-down. The back and seat are upholstered in matching fabric which features a pattern of varied flowers. The backdrop is green, minimally detailed to imply the leaves of the plants. The flowers themselves vary in style with some appearing like peonies, others like daffodils and others as tulips or hydrangeas. The bulk of the florals are pink and white, though some feature blue  instead.
This chair is positioned on the right side of the couch.

title: French Mirror
description: A mirror with a beveled edge set into a wooden frame. The frame is carved with edge columns and arches along the top reminiscent of the repeated tall, narrow arched windows present in French cathedrals. The top of each edge, and the center peak of the arch are both decorated. The lower edge has a repeating rectangular pattern cut into it, similar to the paving stones that would be outside the church. The architectural details of the frame are painted gold, with the recesses of the windows painted black.

title: (1 of 10) Dining Room Side Chair
description:
1 of 10 in a set of side chairs for the dining room table. Each chair is ornately carved on the top of the seat back and at the front Cross-rail. The seat backs are carved in a manner reminiscent of a crest, with two arabesque lines forming a heart or a shield shape at the center. More filigreed lines and florals branch off from the center. Small turned pillars, in a shape akin to a tall vase or ampule, support the seat back. The front crossrail is decorated with arabesque lines akin to those branching off from the shield at the top, though no florals are present a tassel like design can be seen, The wood is varnished with a warm brown stain and the seat is upholstered with a solid golden-colored fabric. Brass rivets hold the upholstery.
1 of 10 chairs - 8 are placed around the dining table, two bracket the china hutch in the dining room. They all appear to be in approximately the same condition and are generally interchangeable with one another.

Donated to Lake Forest College by Robert & Anne Krebs: January 3, 2023.

title: Marble Bench
description: A bench carved from white marble, which has grey veining running through it. The bench seat has four-petaled flowers in anchored circles as a repeating pattern around the rim. Two wide legs support the seat. The leg is carved with a winged lion facing forward and backward so they are mirrored on each leg. Each griffon is depicted with only one paw in the front, though each leg is carved on the side. At the shoulder wings sprout, and the animal itself is depicted with a cat's face, mouth stretched open with a long tongue hanging out.

title: (1 of 4) Floral and Scallop Shell Carved Armchair
description:
An English Style armchair carved extensively with details along most of the wooden surfaces. The back is the most intricate piece with the seat back carved with scallop shells and arabesque leaves ornamenting the borders. An 18-pettled flower with a wide center akin to samplers are carved into the center of the top rail, and four-petaled flowers are depicted at each corner, bordered by more arabesques. The ears, legs and lower crossrail are all turned into the shape of a spiral, with joining blocks carved with flowers with full round petals. The tops and sides are the arm rests are coved, though in lower relief and detail, with a simplified version of the arabesques on the seat back. The wooden sides of the seat match with flowers at the center of each cross-rail. The seat and the center of the backrest are upholstered in a red fabric that is not patterned but has some level of texture to it.
Part of a set of 4 chairs - two are in the living room, one is in the library, one is in the basement. This one is on the right side of the table in the living room.

title: Prie-Dieu Chest of Drawers
description:
A chest of drawers ornately decorated with parquet surfaces or inlays. The chest has three deep drawers, each with their won key and parquet inlays. The whole unit is cut with a sort of divot in the front, and the front of the base will slide out from the rest of the piece. These design choices are likely linked to the use of the object as a Prie-Dieu, allowing spaces for a person to kneel and for their body to fit within the shape of the furniture.
Prie-Dieu (Translated as "Pray to God" From French) Cabinets are used for personal prayer, allowing space in domestic spaces for devotional. title: (1 of 2) Carved Walnut Armchair
description:
An armchair with a high back and low arms. The backrest and seat cushion are fully upholstered. The backrest front is upholstered in a cool green fabric richly patterned with the image of a bouquet in a vase. The seat cushion fabric is similarly adorned with the same types of florals and identical background color. However the base holding the bouquet is different style. The two pieces of fabric are clearly designed to go together. The backing of the seat back is also upholstered in a light green fabric that seems to be some type of water-proof nylon.
The wooden frame is exposed on the arms and legs. The lengths of each section of the frame are left as un-ornamented stained wood, but the focal points (the front of the arm rests, the joinery points and the centers of the cross-rails) are carved with florals and gilt in gold.
Part of a set of two, this chair is on the left.

title: Wooden Drop-Front Desk
description:
An intricately carved desk, with many rounded edges. The sides bow inward and the front is carved into a a series of peaks and dips, with three drawers that follow the same shape of the desk.
The writing front is similarly carved with an inlay that contrasts of two panels of wood with mirrored wood grain. When folded, the writing surface obscures the rest of the writing surface and the upper storage. The upper storage consists of four smaller drawers with pull tabs and an alcove approximately the size of a facial tissue container.
Each drawer has bronze pulls - one each for the smaller upper drawers, and two each for the larger lower drawer.
The front corner is carved with a sort of pillar that sits in front of the rest of the furniture. Areas of parquet inlay create contrast in the wood grain across all the surfaces of the desk. The desk is stained a warm mid-toned brown, looking almost caramel toned in some areas, and slightly darker in the others.

title: Tapestry with Unicorns
description:
A large tapestry woven in golds and reds. The center image depicts two unicorns, facing each other where they both raise up on their rears legs. They stand on either side of an oval medallion, within which are three Fleur de lis. Fabric coils into a roll beneath the medallion, and the fabric is then depicted rising over the medallion and the unicorns draped like the entrance to a tent. Above the medallion and shielded by this drapery is an open crown. At the top of the image a second crown, this one closed with a cap of red fabric, seems to hold the rest of the center imagery aloft. Around the edges architectural arabesques are rendered to appear hollow; the are interspersed with small florals, creating a border around the center image.
This tapestry is paired with a much smaller tapestry, almost half the size, and hung from the long end instead of the short. They depict identical imagery. Both Tapestries are of Modern Construction. Though some elements are highly reminiscent of historic crests - most notably the dual unicorns of the Scottish Coat Of Arms, - the crest depicted does not seem to represent a specific coat of arms from history.

title: Painted Wood Shutter (India)
description:
An oil painting on a wooden shutter. The window frame (boarder) is painted yellow with a repeating four leaf motif and blue and white flowers. Down the center, a wooden beam is painted the same yellow, this time with a repeating white flower and yellow flower pattern.
The shutters depict the book of Yuddha Kanda (sometimes referred to as Landa Kanda), a story within the Sanskrit epic, "Ramayana." This part of the text is about the war between brothers Rama and Lakshmana, and Ravana. The brothers are depicted in the top left panel (Rama is blue-skinned and Lakshmana is tan-skinned), while Ravana is in the top right (he is depicted with multiple faces). Underneath them, on the bottom half of the panels, their respective armies are depicted.
position: N end; to right of alcove

title: Vue de Villefranche sur Mer
description:
A painting of a seaside done on the canvas of a tambourine. The image is done in oil paints and the seaside town is visible at the left of the image in the mid-ground. A group of three sailors is docking a boat - visible immediately in front of the town. They seem to be pulling up to a bank, where yellow and red-brown sand is visible, rather than a dock. The right half of the image shows the sea, stretching out in an inlet with more of the town visible on a far bank through fog or haze.
Title translates to "View of Villefranche-sur-Mer." Villefranche-Sur-Mer is a small town in the Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region on the French Riviera. The village name would translate to Villefranch on sea (or on the sea).

title: Painting of the Holy Family
description: Oil Painting done on copper. A painting of the holy family. The Virgin Mary and infant Jesus dominate the center of the image, with her right arm wrapped around the infant's back to support him. With her left she holds what looks to be the edge of a piece of furniture that has been draped in cloth- potentially a crib or the manger. Christ is turned to look over his shoulder at the viewer. To the right side of the image, over Mary's left shoulder. Saint John holds his crook and looks at the Christ child with his other hand held to his chest in adoration. At the other side, Saint Joseph, Father of Jesus, looks to the child (also presumably in adoration, though the typical posing indicators are hidden due to the view).

title: Madonna col Bambino
description:
Oil painting of the Madonna and Child, done on copper. The Virgin, hooded in glue and gold with a red dress visible underneath holds the infant Christ to her chest. Her left hand supports his back and her right hand lays over her chest as she adores him. Jesus himself seems to be sleeping, with his eyes closed and expression peaceful. His head is tipped to rest on her shoulder and white cloth drapes over him. A thin Halo is visible behind him, and the Virgin has a halo of her own implied by the light backing her head.
Title translates from Italian to "Madonna with Child"

title: Rio Priuli
description:
An oil on canvas depicting the rio ("canal") Priuli in Venice, Italy.
On the right side of the canvas, two boats float in the canal next to a walk-way. The one in the foreground has a brown hull and blue detailing on top. The second boat is a gondola; it is further up the canal, anchored just before a pedestrian bridge. Buildings are on both sides of the canvas. The ones on the left are level with the canal, while the ones on the right side are on a walk-way.
The artist uses thick, heavy brush strokes to create a textured surface.

title: Christ Removing Merchants from the Temple
description:
Oil Painting on Canvas. Christ, dressed in a red robe and blue cloak, stands prominent as the central figure of the painting. His right arm is raised as his left gestures in a point, expelling the Merchants from the Temple. All around him, the merchants cower from him near the borders of the painting. The background is comprised mostly of a large column and wall of the temple itself, although a landscape extends on the left side of the painting. Suggestions of normal life - or at least life as normal before Christ begins his expulsion - are scattered throughout the painting, including the baskets, a chest full of coins and many animals.
The artist is unknown but the skill in rendering the figures and the daily realism of the details reveals a highly skilled artist of Bolognese origin.

title: The Dream of St. Jerome
description:
Oil Painting on Canvas. Depicts Saint Jerome, clutching a cross in the lower right quadrant of the painting. His looks upward, toward where the Virgin Mary is depicted in heaven, attended to by a croup of cherubs. A lone cherub stands with a lion at the lower left side behind the saint. The lion is meant to be his companion, who loyally followed Saint Jerome after he removed a thorn from it's paw.
Saint Jerome was a very important early Christian Scholar during his life. His translation of the Bible into Latin was the standard edition used throughout the Middle Ages, and his influence on monasticism would last for several centuries after his death. It is said that in the spring of 375, Saint Jerome dreamed that he was hauled before a heavenly court and was accused of being a follower of the Roman Philosopher Cicero, rather than a follower of Christ. He was whipped for the crime before waking. After the dream he vowed never to read or own pagan literature again.
The painting can be placed in the Venetian area of the second half of the 18th century, in the circle of G. Diziani.

title: Madonna and Child with Saint John, et al.
description:
Oil Painting on Panel. The Madonna sits at the center of the painting with the infant Christ on her lap. To their left (when viewing), a young Saint John (identified throughout the paperwork in Italian as San Giovannino) holds his Cross in his right hand with his arms crossed over his chest in adoration.
Two people stand with the trio, a man on the left side, and a woman on the right. They are identified as Saint Zachariah, the father of John the Baptist, and either Saint Elisabetta or Anna in documentation. As the female saint holds a book, which is an attribute of Anna (Saint Anne in English), this is her more likely identity. Saint Anne is the mother of the Virgin Mary and grandmother of Jesus Christ.
The Iconography in this image is interesting,as the depiction of a sleeping infant Christ on the Virgin Mary's lap is usually reserved for images of the two of them alone, rather than images of them with other people.
A crack runs through the center of the image, thankfully bypassing the important details of each of the figures. Restoration work has been done periodically on the image.

title: The Last Supper
description:
A Travel Icon from the Cretan School. The image depicts the 12 Apostles, all dressed in blue and red, sat in a helical layout. Christ is present in the image, represented by the symbol "I H S" monogram (shown within the motif of a shining sun) at the lower center of the image. This monogram, along with the sunburst which surrounds it is rendered using the pastiglia technique, so it stands three dimensional above the rest of the scene, which is painted directly onto the flat panel.
The background is a geometric interior, which recedes behind the images of the Apostles. At the top of the panel, the architecture of a decorated arch, along with corner decorations are suggested through the same pastiglia technique as the Monogram of Christ.
The parts of this painting rendered using the pastiglia technique have been all been gilt or painted over in gold.

title: Anatasis (The Resurrection)
description:
An triptych icon, which has been opened and placed into a larger frame. The original Tryptic was rectangular with the frame shaped into an arch at the top. All four hinges appear to be in tact, although the triptych presumably will not close enclosed in the larger frame.
The center panel shows the Descent of Christ to earth following the Resurrection. Within the same panel two additional scenes, one of Christ judgment the souls of men, and one of what might be Christ overseeing a baptism At the top, three haloed angels sit within the arch.
The right panel (when viewing) shows Saint Catherine, dressed in red with gold accents and a blue cloak. A crown sits on her head and she is haloed. Above her, in the arch, stands the Virgin Mary.
The left panel (when viewing) shows Saint Pacôme (Probably in English: Pachomius the Great), dressed in gold and blue. He wears a cap, a long beard and is haloed. Above him, in the arch, stands the Angel Gabriel.

title: Autumn Medley
description:
An oil on canvas. An autumn landscape is depicted. A river begins at the bottom right corner and winds it's way through to the center of the canvas, where it eventually disappears behind a group of trees. The foreground is a small hill on which yellow-leaved birch trees stand. Behind them are pine trees, with a sapling or two in between the birches. In the background is a mountain range. The sky is light blue with fluffy clouds.
Per the name, Christensen depicts an autumn scene. Even the yellow he uses on the birch trees feels cold. The land especially is rendered in a very cool green and yellow-green.

title: La Tete dans les Etoiles
description:
Oil Painting: An abstract painting of a band performing. On the left a musician in black plays the cello, rendered in dull yellows and golds. He is backed by a solid red background on the left hand side of the painting, which transitions to white in the middle and a blue-grey on the right hand side. The right side of the background is accented with a crescent moon and stars in goldenrod. On the right-hand side another musician in green plays the flute, rendered in grey. A singer stands in the middle, dressed in blue with their hands seemingly clasped in front of them. Waving lines cut through he white paint of the background behind the figure may imply either hair or the music the band produces. The paint is slightly textured in it's application.
Title translates to: "Head in the stars" (From French)

title: Madonna and Child with Angels
description:
An oil on canvas. The Virgin Mary is centered and takes up almost the whole height of the canvas. A baby Jesus stands on what appears to be a cloud. He is reaching up toward Mary, on arm around her neck and the other placed on her chest. Mary covers his hand with one of her own, while the other is around his waist.
Mary is dressed in her usual: a red tunic with a blue shawl around her shoulders and a gold-detailed veil atop her head. A few blonde curls fall from under her veil. Jesus is dress in his usual as well: nothing! Like his mother, Jesus has a halo above his blonde curls.
Behind the two is a sea of angelic faces, all appearing to be rather young.
This image is attributed to the Master of the Scandicci Lamentation, whose real name and exact life span remains unknown. He was active in Florence in the 16th century.

description:
A wooden Icon Panel, painted to depict the Madonna and Child. The panel is slightly rounded, so that the virgin and child are presented forward at the apex of the curve. The Virgin is dressed in blue with a hood covering her head, and she holds the infant child with her right hand supporting him against her shoulder. With her left she gestures, either to present or hold the infant Christ, who is dressed in red.
The background is painted a solid color, rather than detailed, but has been adorned with a small metal decoration that has been nailed into the painting on either side of the virgin. A frame made of the same metal (Type unclear) has been added to the panel. It is not clear if the frame is contemporaneous to the image, but it was clearly made for this piece specifically as it is molded to fit the arch of the panel, and has been cut to indicate the shape of a Halo around the virgins's head. The frame has been stamped or etched with geometric patterns and shows signs of ware, including a missing chunk of metal near the center of the bottom frame.

title: Crucifixion
description:
A large wooden Icon Panel, painted to depict the Crucifixion. The center of the image is dominated by an inlaid metal cross, (likely brass?). The cross has been carved with a detail of Christ crucified, although the crown of thorns has been omitted in favor of showing a halo. The nails through his feet and palms are detailed. Above his head angels look down toward Christ. At his feet a small detail of city or fortress towers extends to either side and a scull is seemingly buried at his feet. The rest of the panel is painted depicting the scene of the crucifixion and what follows.
To his left stands three women. While it is not confirmed, these figures are presumably the Three Marys to witness the crucifixion (the Virgin Mary, Mary Magdalen, and Mary Clopas). All three are haloed and wear blue/green dresses. The right-most of the trio looks toward the crucifixion with her hand raised to her face as if Crying. The central figure stands behind the other two, looking away from the crucifixion. Both of these women have shawls that wrap over the head which are a dark, wine-red color. The third figure, to the left side of the trio, also has the same style shawl, but it is bright rid. She also gazes toward the scene of the crucifixion.
To the right side of the inlaid cross, stand two more onlookers to the crucifixion. The first figure is a haloed woman. She is dressed in a green dress with a bright red shawl, but it is not warped, leaving her hair uncovered. Her identity is unconfirmed, but her lack of a veil suggests she may be Veronica. To the right of this female saint is a soldier, also haloed. He is dressed in armor, a red cloak with a white hood and boots. His identity is also unconfirmed, but as he carries a spear he may be interpreted as Longinus.
Above the cross in the upper left hand corner of the image The Descent from the Cross is depicted: six people work to lower Christ from the cross. On the left of the cross stand two of the women from the trio in the lower scene: The woman with the bright shawl and the crying women in dark red. To the right, the same male and female unidentified saints. At the top two new figures work to lower Christ from the cross. These new figures are also haloed, and are traditionally identified as Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, though their identities are unconfirmed here.

title: Jesus, Mary and Saints in Landscape.
description:
Wooden Icon Panel painted to show Jesus, Mary an angel and several Saints standing in a landscape. Jesus can be identified sitting atop a cloud in the upper left side of the painting. Mary, also atop a cloud, floats in the center of the upper half of the painting. An Angel in a red cloak, holding what might be spear stands beneath her, at ground level, but is also depicted to be standing atop clouds. Surrounding the angel stand four saints, four on each side. Five are women, but the three lower left-most figures on either side of the angel are men. None of the saints are identifiable by their iconography, but there is faded writing on the painting that may lend clues to their identities if it can be translated. The saints stand four to each side, with two on the ground, and two seeming to float in space behind them. This is presumably done to assist with the composition as they are pointedly not depicted standing on clouds like the figures of Jesus, Mary and the angel.

title: Mother of God Galaktotrophousa
description:
Known in English as either an Icon of The Virgin as "the Milk-Giver" or The Virgin Nursing. The image is a painted wooden Icon panel that depicts an infant Christ held in the arms of the Virgin as he drinks from her breast.
The Virgin is depicted wearing a blue dress with a red hooded cloak - a transparent white veil can also be seen underneath the hood. She supports the infant Christ, holding him up to right side. Her head is tilted toward him, but her gaze is directed to the viewer. Christ himself is dressed in white and gold. He sits upright in his mother's arms, with both hands grasping her breast to drink. His Gaze is directed up toward his mother.
The motif of the nursing Madonna was found in early Christian Mythology, and is an evocative representation of the human nature of the son of God. References to he theme can be found in Byzantine homilies and hymns with comparisons drawn between the milk from Mary's breast and the blood from Jesus' side. The comparison links the two theologically and creates a connection between the Mother of God Galaktotrophousa and Christ's suffering on the cross.
The background of this painting is golden, but a halo is implied around the duo by a pattern punched into the surface. In order to produce this motif, the punch would be placed perpendicular to the gold surface, then struck to produce a slight indent in the gesso beneath. This had to be done when the gesso was still soft to prevent damaging the gold leaf which constitutes the top layer.

title: Christ Pantocrator Enthroned
description:
Large wooden Icon Panel, painted to depict Christ Pantocrator Enthroned. In the image, Christ sits enthroned, with his feet resting on a footstool. Dressed in an ocher yellow robe he looks toward the viewer with his right hand raised in a blessing, typical of the Pantocrator image. In his left hand he balances a gospel open on his knee. The book shows Matthew 11, 28: Come unto me, all ye that labor and are heavy laden and I will give you rest. (The writing is in Slavic and has bene translated, courtesy of Authenticator Dr. S.G. Morskin).
Around Christ the celestial world is depicted. It is comprised of many layers that together across the image and come together to symbolize the universe: The inner red diamond shape symbolizes heavenly fire (heaven of Heavens) where God resides. This is surrounded by an oval of blue, within which a motif depicting the faces and wings of seraphim (six-winged angels) is repeated. Where these figured hover, refers to heaven, behold which a red rectangle symbolizes the earth.
At the feet of Christ Thrones are depicted. In the traditional hierarchy, these angels, (together with Seraphim an cherubim) belong to the highest order of angels. They are typically depicted as circles (filled with eyes) which perpetually revolve and are propelled by small wings.
At each corner the symbols of the four evangelists are each drawn looking toward their neighbor: The Angel for Matthew in the upper left corner, the eagle for Mark in the upper right, the lion for John in the lower left and the ox for Luke in the lower left. Each depiction holds a gospel book, though these ones are closed. (Note that the allocation of these symbols are of the Orthodox Tradition, which differs from the western one where the Eagle would represent John and the Lion would represent Mark.)
Around the borders of this image restoration has resulted in the background being stripped to reveal the gesso ground.
Byzantine inspired. Eastern Orthodox Church. Central Russia.

title: Saints Basil and Stefania
description:
Wooden icon panel painted to present the image of two saints. Both are haloed and stand facing each one another. Saint Basil is presented on the left side of the image. He is presented with his typical attributes: depicted as having a long, dark beard that tapers to a point, he is draped in the vestments of a Pope and holds a book. The book is in his left hand and his right had is raised to bless Saint Stephanie, who he looks toward.
Saint Stefania (more commonly spelled Stefana or Stephanie) stands dressed in gold and red with a white hood covering her hair. She holds a cross in her right hand and gestures toward Basil, as if to accept or return his blessing, with her left.
The background is presented as a tiled floor and a wall with a pattern that looks to also be brick or tile, as if they are inside. Above them, at the center of the painting, Christ sits in heaven, clouds beneath him, and raises a hand to each of the saints, granting each of them a blessing. The borders of the painting seem to be rendered with metal, or in a very thick metallic paint, though it does not wrap the sides of the panel. The metal is etched with a scrolling vine patterns. Painted bundles of fruit and leaves decorate the corners, sides and bottom.
14/15 Icons featured on the main wall of the South hall Gallery: Bottom, second from Right.

title: Mother of God Pecerskaja with Saints Boris and Gleb
description:
Wooden icon panel painted with the images of the Virgin Mary holding the infant Christ and two Saints standing in attendance. The two saints are identified as Boris and Gleb, (Boris, the elder is probably the one on the left). They stand on either side of the Virgin and child, dressed alike except that the one on the left is bearded and bears a red cloak. The one on the right is clean shaven and wears a white cloak.
The Virgin and child sit enthroned at the center of the image. The virgin holding the Christ child in her lap. They both face the viewer, and the Christ Child raises both of his hands in blessing, one for each of the saints at their sides.
The saints are often depicted together as they were, as a pair, the first canonized saints in Kievan Rus (modern day Russia) following the state's adoption of Christianity (canonized 1071). According to 11th century stories Boris and Gleb were the younger sons of Vladimir the Great (r. 980-1015). Both of the brothers are regarded as having been pious and were venerated following their individual assassinations and martyrdoms during the internecine wars (1015–1019).
15/15 Icons featured on the main wall of the South hall Gallery: Bottom, far right.

title: Mystic Marriage of Saint Catherine
description:
An oil on canvas depicting the Mystic Marraige of St. Catherine. The Marraige ceremony is a common theme in Christian art, though it should be noted that there are two Saint Catherines (St. Catherine of Alexandria and St. Catherine of Sienna), both of whom may be the Saint depicted in the ceremony. Rarely they are depicted together, but this image is typical depicting Saint Catherine, crouched with her hand presneted to an infant christ. The infant sits on the Virgin Mary's lap, placing a ring on Catherine's finger. In the background two angels observe the scene.
St. Catherine of Alexandria is the Saint depicted in the Maratti image in the LFC collection. She can be identified both by her clothes - lavish dresses of yellow, white and gold with a jeweled band in her hair - as well as by the positioning of christ - who places a ring on her finger. Both the ring and her depiction as a princess identifies this Saint as Catherine of Alexandria. (Saint Catheirne of Siena is typically depicted as a Nun in the habit of the Domincan Order with the black over-robe open in the front.)
Saint Catherine of Alexandria was born in the 3rd Century C.E. in Alexandria, Roman Egypt. According to her hagiography she was both a princess and a scholar. Around the age of 14 she converted to Christianity after having a vision of the Virgin Mary and Christ. In the visoin she wed Christ, leading to the foundation of the mystic marraige. She remained a virgin as a result of this marraige. She is credited with converting hundreds of others. At the age of 18 she was martyred, following toture at the hands of Roman Emperor Maxentius. Notably, she is also identified as one of the Saints who appeared to Joan of Arc in the 15th century.

Rarely they are depicted together, but this image is typical depicting Saint Catherine, crouched with her hand presneted to an infant christ. The infant sits on the Virgin Mary's lap, placing a ring on Catherine's finger. In the background two angels observe the scene.
St. Catherine of Alexandria is the Saint depicted in the Maratti image in the LFC collection. She can be identified both by her clothes - lavish dresses of yellow, white and gold with a jeweled band in her hair - as well as by the positioning of christ - who places a ring on her finger. Both the ring and her depiction as a princess identifies this Saint as Catherine of Alexandria. (Saint Catheirne of Siena is typically depicted as a Nun in the habit of the Domincan Order with the black over-robe open in the front.)
Saint Catherine of Alexandria was born in the 3rd Century C.E. in Alexandria, Roman Egypt. According to her hagiography she was both a princess and a scholar. Around the age of 14 she converted to Christianity after having a vision of the Virgin Mary and Christ. In the visoin she wed Christ, leading to the foundation of the mystic marraige. She remained a virgin as a result of this marraige. She is credited with converting hundreds of others. At the age of 18 she was martyred, following toture at the hands of Roman Emperor Maxentius. Notably, she is also identified as one of the Saints who appeared to Joan of Arc in the 15th century. | Oil Paint | Italian | 17th Century | Painting | Dining Room

title: Saints Constantine and Helena (Icon)
description:
Wooden icon panel painted to depict Saints Constantine and Helena. The tow stand side by side, both dressed in red robes with elaborate trims and belts. They are both crowned as well as haloed and they hold a cross upright between them. The background is painted or foiled with gold. The panel is carved so that the edge sits slightly above the ground where the figures are painted, implying both a border and a degree of separation between the Saints and the image.
Saint Constantine is also known in history as Constanine I or Constantine the Great. He stands on the left hand side of the image. A roman Emperor, Constantine converted to Christianity in 312, and in 313 oversaw proclamation of the Edict of Milan, which declared religious tolerance to all Christians within the empire. He was respected by both the medieval church as a paragon of virtue, and by contemporary secular rulers as a prototype. During his reign he also founded Constantinople on the ancient city of Byzantium (modern Istanbul) and made it the Capitol of the Eastern Roman Empire. He is venerated in most Christian denominations as a Saint.
On the Right hand statement stands Saint Helena, Constantine's mother. She converted to the faith following her son's conversion. She is venerated in the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Asian Orthodox and Anglican churches, as well as commemorated in the Lutheran tradition. Her major role as a saint is as the patron of Archaeologists and new discoveries, having been given this title due to her efforts to recover Christian relics during her lifetime. Constantine gave her unlimited access to the Roman Empire's treasury to fund these relic hunting journeys and she went on several pilgrimages looking for relics with the aid of these funds. According to tradition, in approximately 326 Helena completed a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Here, she oversaw the tearing down of a temple to Venus, which was thought to be built over the tomb of Jesus. During this work she discovered the True Cross, which was then brought to Rome and is the most common attribute used to identify her in artistic renditions.

title: Tree of Jesse (Icon)
description:
Wooden Icon panel. Painted with the image of the Tree of Jesse. The tree of Jesse is a Christian motif which was very popular during the Medieval period. It's use has continued to the modern day. Depictions of the tree show the Biblical genealogy of the Jesus Christ as it descends from Jesse, the father of King David.
Inspiration for the Tree of Jesse comes from a passage in Issiah: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots" (King James Version).
The Chrismon tree and the Advent calendar are sometimes referred to by modern Christians as the Jesse Tree, though this practice does not relate to the original genealogical depiction. In Advent and Chrisom traditions see the decoration of a real tree or poster with 'Chisoms' symbols representing the stories that lead up to Christmas.

title: Entombment of Christ
description:
A circular icon painting with a carved frame, painted on panel. The image depicts Christ, who is being wrapped in a white shroud and lowered into a coffin. Nicodemus and Saint Joseph of Arimathea are the ones to lower him, one at the shoulders, the other at the feet. The Virgin Mary, dressed in a red hooded cloak and robes, stands at the center of the image. She holds Christ's hand as he is lowered. Mary Magdalen, also hooded in red, though her dress beneath is blue, knees at Christ's feet with a golden cup held in her hands.
Behind the group who interacts with the body, three more saints are fathered. Saint John stands at the Virgin's left shoulder. The other two figures are identified as spice-bearing female martyrs - the spice in question is probably Myrrh, which would have been used to anoint the body. The identities of these women is difficult to pinpoint, as many Biblical women have been identified as the ones to anoint the body in different denominations and records.
At the very back of the group of figures two angels stand at the corners. The angels depict night and day, the one the left having blue wings, and the one on the left having red. The cross stands over the group as a whole, and god is depicted in heaven above. There is no background, but the foreground is painted to depict the ground.

title: Ark going to Jerusalem
description:
A wooden icon panel. It is painted to depict a procession headed into a city. Tall walls surround the buildings, which only have their rooftops visible. One of the buildings has the red, domed roof of a church. Another has a blue-tiled roof and a man dressed in red stands watching the procession from a balcony. he appears to be haloed, and is probably a second image of the haloed king who stands at the center of the procession and image.
This man, probably King David, wears a grown and a red cape over a blue robe, both of which are more ornamented than the rest of the people in the procession. He plays a psaltery (a triangular stringed instrument that may be bowed, though in this image the man plays through a method of plucking).
Aside from this central figure, the procession consists mainly of men and women playing instruments, but additional figures include a man dressed in white who leads the oxen cart, and two figures dressed in blue (likely the same man depicted twice). In one version of the man, he holds a walking stick and reaches up to place his hand upon the Ark. In the second he lies upon the ground with his eyes closed, dead. Based on this depiction, the man might be Uzzah, who is said to have touched the Ark in an attempt to steady it when the cart tilted, and was immediately struck dead by God for the error.
The Ark itself is in the oxen drawn cart. It is painted mostly golden, but is also depicted as if it is encrusted in jewels. Red orbs hover near it, each with multiple wings coming off of them. This may be meant to depict the six-winged Seraphs. At the top of the image an orb ringed in gold is depicted with three rays coming off in the direction of the Ark, showing the connection between the Ark and heaven.

title: The Three Kings Offering Presents to the Newborn Christ
description:
Wooden icon panel, painted to depict the scene of the three kings going to visit the new born Christ. The kings are shown in the lower right hand corner of the painting, all three are crowned and they ride on a black, brown and white stallion respectively. The first king raises his hand to indicate the direction of the Christ child.
Beside them, St. Joseph kneels beside a river, tending to the animals from the manger where the Christ child was born. A young man plays a horn nearby. Angels fly amongst the scene, descending from heaven, depicted as an arch carved into the top of the image, where further angels sit among the clouds. Rays of golden light connect the clouded scene to the head of Christ.
At the upper left corner, the baby Jesus lays swaddled and covered by the roof of the manger. An ox lays it's head upon the boy, regarding him, and the Virgin kneels praying over the child. The Holy family are all haloed, as are the angels, though their haloes are significantly smaller. The kings and the boy are not haloed.

title: Three Kings Visiting the Newborn Christ
description:
Wooden Icon panel, depicting the Three Kings presenting gifts to the newborn Christ. In the image the Holy Family stands together on the right side of the image. All three are haloed, with the Christ child sitting on the Virgin's lap, and St. Joseph watching over the Virgin's shoulder.
The first king, a Caucasian man dressed in red with a long white beard kneels at the feet of the virgin and presents the first gift of Gold to Christ. He has removed his crown, which sits on a pillow beside them. A money box sits on the ground between them, open so the gold within is visible.
The Second king bows so that he is below the eye-line of saint Joseph, he hold the incense bowl for frankincense before himself. He is depicted with a short grey beard and he is cloaked in red.
The Third king is a black man with no facial hair and a crown still on his head. He is dressed in red and blue and he presents Myrrh to the Holy Family. The Myrrh is in circular vessel, and he carries a stem of the plant in his other hand.
Above the scene the sky is depicted golden and heaven stand out depicted with a circular symbol in the upper left corner. Rays of light come of fin the direction of the Christ child, depicting his connection to the heavenly realm.

title: Corn Husking in Santa Fe
description:
Two women sit in a cart. They are husking corn, and a very large woven basket has been set between the wheels of the cart on the side facing the audience. The basket is meant to collect the corn husks, and is currently overflowing with an excess of the husks collecting around the front wheel. The husked corn cobbs are in a pile in the back of the cart.
The two women sit, both dressed in white collared shirts and bonnets. They are turned toward each other, as if talking while they work. More figures are visible in the background, but they are out of focus. The cart itself is fitted with a wood shaft that would allow the cart to be hitched to a horse or oxen team, though it does not appear to be attached currently. It looks like the women and their cart are sitting in a sort of courtyard, with a building partially visible in the background and a lowe fence encircling the rest of the background.

title: Five Paintings of the Life of Christ
description:
Five Scenes from the life of Christ. The set appears to have gone together originally, but the frame to display them together is a modern commission specifically designed to house them.
The first scene is the Annunciation of the Virgin Mary (From Luke 1). The Virgin is depicted sitting to the right side of the image. At the left, an Angel, (Gabriel) approaches her, and a dove is suspended the air above them both, symbolizing the holy spirit. This is a common composition for the iconography.
The second image depicts a Young Jesus in the Temple (Luke 2). In this scene his parents find the young man surrounded by teachers from the temple, where he has been learning for 3 days. All those who observed the scene were amazed by his understanding.
The third scene shows an adult Jesus standing among his sleeping apostles. An Angel is presenting a vision, probably the one he has in Luke 9 of his covenant and death. The angel holds a cross and a chalice.
The fourth scene depicts the torture of Jesus Christ at the hands of Pontius Pilot and his men. This is from Mark 15 and precedes his crucifixion. Two men whip his back as he stands looking forlorn with his arms tied behind his back.

title: #30 Archway, Cotignac
description: A painting of a side street in Cotignac, France. The path of the street is paved with square tiles, which follow a slope down to the center of the image. The viewer stands looking in an intersection of this side street with another. A set of stairs disappears around the side of the building to the right. The intersecting street curves in from the left before the intersection before continuing forward, up the center of the painting. An archway for a building spans the width of the street. A window is cut in the wall of the span, which is adorned with flowers growing from a window planter. Other greenery sprouts from pots and planters all around the scene. Visible beyond the arch, a man and a woman stop in the street to speak with one another.

title: Santa Croce
description:
An oil painting image of the Basilica di Santa Croce (Basilica of the Holy Cross). It is pictured from the front, with it's bell tower on the right side and the plaza stretching out in front of it. The building is the home of the principal Franciscan chapter in Florence.
The Chapel is seen from the Piazza di Santa Croce, with it's Gothic Revival Facade, which was added in the years between 1857 and 1863. The new Facade was designed by Niccolò "Nicola" Matas, a Jewish architect from Acona (6 December 1798 – 11 March 1872). He is responsible for the working of the prominent Star of David at the top of the church and was buried at the threshold to the church, (his tomb was placed there as a means to avoid buying a Jewish man on the catholic consecrated grounds of the church).
The dome of the Pazzi Chapel is visible in the background on the right side. Long shadows are cast over the plaza, which is full of people, indicating the late hour as sun begins to set. The entire scene is bathed in s a soft warm light which reflects off the white facade.

title: Old Trading Post
description:
An oil on canvas. Depicted is an old-fashioned trading post. It's made up of wooden stalls placed wall-to-wall. A woman stands in front of the trading post, dressed in a red dress and a gray or blue head covering and shawl. The trading post and the woman are in the mid-ground of the left side of the painting. A tree directly to the right of the post divides the composition in two.
Just to the right of the tree are two figures. They are too far away to make out, although one appears to be a woman in a similar shawl as the first. A small house or shed is to the far right, on the edge of the canvas.
In the background we see purple mountains; in the foreground, patches of dehydrated grass.

title: Paris at Dawn
description:
An oil on canvas. Depicted is Paris as the sunrises. In the center of the painting, a woman stands on a cobblestone street. She appears to have a red or pink bonnet on. To the right of the painting, a horse and carriage and its driver. Besides the woman, they are the only people on the street.
In the left foreground is a tall, leafless tree, planted in the sidewalk. There are two buildings on either side of the figures; they start in the left and right corners respectively and begin to head toward the mid-ground on a slight diagonal. There are buildings on the left and right of the figures; there is a gap between the two where the viewer is able to see into the background. Otherwise, the buildings and tree obscure the audience's view.

title: Greek Icon "Stories of Elijah"
description:
A large Icon depicting Scenes from the life of the Prophet Elijah.
Elijah enters the Bible in the Book of Kings by challenging the goddess Baal and her priests, and Ahab, the king of Israel. The challenge comes in the form of a prophecy of a drought, which goes against the powers of Baal, who oversees a domain of rain, thunder, lightning and dew.
The first scene depicted in the panel follows his challenge and a subsequent warning from God to flee Israel. The city can be seen in the distance on the left side of the image. Following God's instructions he seeks shelter by a brook east of the Jordan River. A wide body of water flows down the left side of the panel away from Israel.
Once the brook dries, Elijah follow's god's instructions to proceed to Zarephath in Phoenicia. There, he is put up in the house of and fed by one of the City's Widows. A miracle is performed wherein her flour and oil do not run out and then Elijah raises her son from the dead after he passes away during Elijah's stay. This Scene does not seem to be depicted in the panel.
After 3 years, god foretells the end of the drought and the famine and instructs Elijah to return to Israel and once again challenge Baal and Ahab. His Challenge takes the form of two sacrifices of a bull. One prepared for Baal and another prepared for Yahweh. Both Bulls are prepared and lead to a pyre, and prayers are said for the wood to light. Baal's prophets attempt to light the pyre to no effect, but when Elijah prays a ball of fire falls from the sky ignite his sacrifice. Elijah can be seen praying next to the fire in the lower right of the image. In the Bible the followers of Baal declare for Yahweh and kill the prophets of Baal.
This story ends with Elijah's explosion form Israel by Jezebel, resulting in days spent wandering the wilderness of Beersheba. During this time he travels to Mount Horeb, where Abraham received the 10 commandments. This scene is depicted at the center left of the panel. Elijah wanders, holding his cloak over his head to shield him from the sun as he makes his journey to seek out the lord.
During this Journey, he faces trials of wind, fire and earthquakes and the story continues to take Elijah to a final confrontation with Ahaziah, the son of Ahab. Ahaziah sends three men to try and capture Elijah, but he strikes two of them down with fire called from the sky. When the third man asks for mercy, Elijah agrees to of with him. Ahaziah dies according to a prophecy spoken by Elijah, from injuries sustained in a fall. This scene is again no depicted in the panel.
Elijah's story comes to an end in 2 Kings 2:3-9, where his ascending to heaven is witnessed by Elisha. In the scene a chariot of fire drawn by horses descends to earth, and Elijah is taken away in a whirlwind, leaving behind his mantel for Elisha to catch. This scene is depicted across the upper half of the Panel. Elijah himself rising, haloed and directing the horses, who are the same color as the fiery chariot on which he sits. He is Haloed and looks to the shining rays of Heaven at the top of the panel. Elijah is depicted taking his Mantel at the lower right of the Panel.

title: Winding River at Twilight
description:
A painting mounted as a Tryptic with hinged panels. The center image of the opened center depicts the river winding toward the viewer in wide swings.
A tree grows at one of the bends. The river crosses onto the left panel, with another tree visible at the edge of the painting with another tree seen at the edge of the high bank.
After swinging back into the center panel, the river then disappears behind the lip of the bank as seen from the perspective of the viewer where it stretches across the bottom of the center and right side panels.
When the Tryptic is closed, the two exterior panels show more of the landscape, father out from the focal point of the River, which is no longer visible.
A small fourth panel sits as an arch above the center panel, in which the twilight sky is clear enough to see the first sign of the moon.

title: White Marble Pedestal
description:
A carved White Marble Pedestal, which supports the statue of Suzanna in the back yard. The Pedestal itself is carved with scenes depicting her story.
Also called Suzanna and the elders, the story is told of a beautiful young woman. In the privacy of her walled garden, Suzanna bathes, but is spied by two elders of the village, both of whom covet her. Working together they try to bribe her into having sex, threatening to say she has committed adultery if she refuses. When she refuses, the elders hold to the threat and make a public accusation of adultery. It is only after the two men are cross-examined by Daniel and reveal discrepancies in their stories that Suzanna is proven innocent.
Suzanna's story is only considered to be canonical in the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches.In these denominations the story is part of the book of Daniel. In most other denominations of Christianity, Suzanna's story is not considered cannon, but it is considered to be useful for teaching. The motif of the story is very common in artwork. Images depicting the tale date back to as early as the 9th century. It was particularly popular in the 15th and 16th centuries. When painted the image usually depicts Suzanna and the two voyeurs in a scene. When sculpted in the round, Suzanna is usually depicted alone.
In the context of Krebs House, the Suzanna statue (KR23.2.27) sits atop the White Marble Pedestal (KR23.3.10), framed by a Italian Stone Rotunda (KR23.3.11), and set as the focal point of a fountain.

title: 19th Century Marble Column Pedestal
description:
An elaborately carved white marble pillar, standing more than 5 feet tall. On the pillar, sections are carved. The base is curled to present as large leaves. Above that the lowest section of the pillar is carved to show birds and foliage. Above that a narrow band shows grape vines and leaves are carved to stand in the round out from the pillar. Another section is carved to show narrower leaves, akin to those at the base. This is followed by a larger section at the top, at the base of which four male heads are carved. Each face is the same, with long curly hair and a full mustache and beard. Branches of a fruiting tree with fanning leaves (maybe olives?) are sculpted into the rest of the section above their heads. Then the capital.
The pillar supports an Italian Terracotta Bust of a woman (entered separately as KR23.2.8a).

title: Spring
description:
A terracotta statue of Spring, envisioned as a young woman. Draped in a toga, and barefoot with her hair pulled up in a bun at the top of her neck. She holds a bouquet of leaves and roses at her left hip.
Made from a high quality terracotta that fires to the typical rose color while being highly resistant to frost and ice. Molded by hand from a 'baco' cylinder of clay (also called a worm) by artisans at the Manifattura Impruneta Workshop in Italy. Once the item is sculpted it is dried naturally for approximately 30 days before being fired for 72 hours in a kiln that reaches approximately 1,050 degrees centigrade.
Matches 4 other sculptures in the yard (one for each season), though they don't seem to have all been purchased at the same time. This sculpture is positioned near the mailbox at the driveway entrance.

title: Marble Statue of a Warrior
description:
Statue carved from a mix of white and red marble. The warrior himself is carved from the white stone, he stands contrapposto and gazes just to his left. His hair is cut short and held down next to his head with a band. He has a short but full beard and mustache. His physique is traditional to Greek and roman sculptures with defined, well proportioned muscles. From the base of the statue a tree trunk is cut of at mid- thigh to act as additional support for the warrior.
The red marble is carved into a drapery that falls from his left shoulder, draping across the back and down the left side of the body. It is draped over his left wrist. The two pieces of marble seem to have been carved completely separately then joined after the fact. It is unclear exactly how this joining took place.

title: Bronze Statue of Moses (after Michelangelo)
description:
A Bronze cast statue after Michelangelo's Moses. The statue is rendered in a very high degree of detail showing Moses with short hair, but a very long beard, which curls in tendrils down his chest and is met by the fingers of his hand. Seated on a large block, the right foot is planted in front of the body, and the left is angled back toward his side. Under his right arm two tablets (Those which presented the ten commandments) are propped, held in place on the stone. He is dressed in a sleeveless tunic, which gathers in large pleats and drapes over his lap, leaving defined, muscular arms and the lower legs and sandaled feet exposed.
The original Statue by Michelangelo was commissioned by Pole Julius II for his tomb. The commission took 40 years to complete, 1505-1545. Pope Julius died in 1513 and did not see the completion of the tomb. It is carved from marble and stands approximately 3x the size of the bronze at Krebs House.

title: St. Francis of Assisi
description:
Bronze statue depicting St. Francis of Assisi. He stands with a tall posture, though his attention is cast downward, as if he is looking at someone or something that is shorter than him. His face is kind and open, and he has a shortly cropped beard and mustache. He is dressed in the traditional Franciscan Habit of a long robe tied at the waist with a rope. St. Francis' hood is down, showing his Tonsure. Two birds have perched on him, one on the right wrist, the other in his left hand.
St. Francis is the patron of Animals, Merchants and Ecology and his Feast-Day is on February 4th. Born in Assisi in Umbria (Modern Italy), he is best known as the founder of the Franciscan monastic order. His father was a merchant, and tradition says he had an easy-going temperament and happy manner. Francis' conversion from a man of business to a man of God followed a failed attempt at the Crusades, from which he returned without seeing battle. He eventually found himself at a Church at San Damiano, where the image of Christ on the crucifix implored him to repair the Chapel.

title: (1/2) Bronze relief after Donatello
description:
Bronze relief of a young angel. His body pushes forward from the frame, though his feet are planted behind the bottom of the frame. He is turned over his left shoulder, and the right wing peaks past the edge of the frame. He is blowing a trumpet, which is aimed up and back behind the frame in the direction that he is facing. He wears a tunic and is haloed with short hair.
This relief is a modern loose rendering of the same image by Donatello. The original bronzes are a set of 12 musical angels, which adorn the High Altar at the Basilica di Sant’Antonio, Padua. The originals are rendered in more detail than the recreations in LFC's collections. The originals are slightly larger, approximately 22.8"H x 8.3"W.

title: (1/2) Bronze relief of a Biblical Scene
description:
A bronze relief depicting a Biblical scene. At the right of the image a man faces right, holding a cane in his left hand and leading a donkey with his left. He is bearded and slightly hunched forward. Atop the donkey sits, two figures, a woman and a child who ride side saddle with the child in the woman's lap. There is not background, but there is a low border, which may have at one time been rivetted into another support.
It's difficult to identify which Bible story this may relate to. The composition of man, woman and child usually can imply the Holy Family, however the usual references of Mary riding a Donkey are on the road to Bethlehem, before Christ is born.

description:

The two figures hold leaves over themselves, and the one on the right crosses one arm over her chest to cover it. Around the figures tall, stalked branching plants are depicted as the background.
The scene is very likely the expulsion of Adam and Eve from the Garden of Eden.

title: Madonna and Child
description:
Stucco Bas-relief of the Madonna and Child. The image was created by Antonio Rossellino and his workshop in Ferrara. This particular image seems to sit between Rossellino's early mature style - defined by vibrant and dynamic compositions - and his later style - known for more severe and solid image productions.
It is ascribed to be part of the "Candelabra Madonnas," a group of works by Rossellino which are identified by the consistent depiction of two lighted candelabras in the background of the image. The shared prototype of the Candelabra images is a terracotta bas-relief, which is currently housed at the Victoria and Albert museum and dated between 1465 and 1470. Two sizes of exist within this group, the larger set of which almost identically match the Prototype. However, the image in the LFC collection belongs in the smaller size group, which tends to show variations from the original and between each piece.

title: Coronation of the Virgin (Model in Clay)
description:
A bozzetto, or rough clay sculpture, done as a model in prepreparation of a larger piece. In this case, the final work was probably intended to be an altarpiece. The image depicts the Virgin Mary being coronated as the Queen of Heaven.
Mary herself is pictured twice. Once in the bottom half of the image, she is depicted on earth, kneeling before a group of saints who observe her coronation. Second, in the upper half of the image, she kneels to receive the crown in Heaven.
Alongside her in the upper half of the sculpture the Holy Trinity is depicted, ready to anoint her with the crown. Jesus the son crouches on the left side of the image, indicated by the cross behind him; it seems to be supported by his left arm which is not shown in the relief. His right hand supports the crown. God the father sits on the right hand side. His right hand holds up the crown, and his left rests on a globe, probably meant to depict the world, which is supported by a cherub. The Holy Spirit is depicted above the scene as a dove, flying as a focal point at the top of the image.
The earthly scene depicts the Virgin, almost directly beneath the upper image so they are both centered, though the earthly image seems positioned slightly to the side by the forward push of the saints depicted along the left side of the image. From left to right in the front row, the Attending Saints are identified as: Saint John Nepomuk, Saint Dominic, A praying female saint (Probably Catherine of Siena, but could also be Saint Theresa). In the back row of saints who move from left to right, behind the Virgin: A male saint who holds himself upright with a cane in his left hand (Probably Francis of Paola, but could also be Antony the Abbot/Antony the Great), Saint Joachim, Saint Anne, and Saint Appolonia (holding a tooth). Saint John the Baptist stands to the right side of the Virgin with his right hand raised over her, as if he is doing the earthly anointing.

title: Night (After Michelangelo)
description:
A replica of Michelangelo's Night, carved in Alabaster. Both the original and the replica in the LFC collection are part of set, though their counterparts are not the same between the sets.
The image of Night depicts a woman lounged leaning on her left arm. The right leg is relaxed, following the shape of the arch on which she sits. Her left leg is drawn up to support the right arm, on which her head is leaned in turn. Tipped down, as if to use the arm to block the light, the figure's eyes are closed, sleeping. Her hair is drawn back, using a band to keep it away from her face, though some of it falls back over her left shoulder. The pose is serene in it's stillness.
The recreations in the LFC collection are significantly smaller than the original images, which adorn the Tomb of Giuliano de Medici. The original Night Sculpture was carved between 1526 and 1531 and is approximately 59" x 60". Likely as a result of the change in size, the replicas have been simplified, including the removal of an owl, who sits in the crook of Night's elevated leg in the original. It adorns the left side of the Sarcophagus and is accompanied on the right side by a depiction of Day - rendered as a man lounging in the opposite direction. All of the original statues were carved in Marble and are still installed in the Medici Chapel in Florence. The two figures of Night and Dawn are the only two female nudes ever depicted by Michelangelo.

title: Dawn (after Michelangelo)
description:
A replica of Michelangelo's Dawn, carved in Alabaster. Both the original and the replica in the LFC collection are part of set, though their counterparts are not the same between the sets.
The image of Dawn depicts a woman lounged leaning on her right arm. The right leg is relaxed, following the shape of the arch on which she sits. Her left leg is drawn up as if she is getting ready push off from her recline and stand. Her hair is drawn up in a turban, which the left arm reaches up to adjust off of her shoulder. Her head is turned up, and the face is furrowed as if worried, highlighting deep-set eyes and a frown on her mouth. Her figure is nude, except for a band which wraps around the base of her chest, below the breasts. The band is typical of Slave's garments at the time.
The recreations in the LFC collection are significantly smaller than the original images, which adorn the Tomb of Lorenzo de Medici. The original Dawn Sculpture was carved between 1520 and 1534 and is approximately 69" x 92". The replica image has been simplified, likely due to the significant reduction in size. It adorns the right side of the Sarcophagus and is accompanied on the right side by a depiction of Dusk - rendered as a man lounging in the opposite direction. All of the original statues were carved in Marble and are still installed in the Medici Chapel in Florence. The two figures of Night and Dawn are the only two female nudes ever depicted by Michelangelo.

title: Susanna
description:
A statue of Suzanna, as lifted from her story within the Bible. She is seated, pitched forward, and looking over her shoulder, moving to cover herself as she realizes her uninvited audience. She is draped in patterned fabrics that sit low around her waist, and her hair is held up with a scarf. Earrings are her only other adornments as she holds herself on the rockwork base, which is carved with foliage. At her feet a stream runs.
The story of Suzanna is one commonly depicted in art. Also called Suzanna and the elders, the story is told of a beautiful young woman. In the privacy of her walled garden, Suzanna bathes, but is spied by two elders of the village, both of whom covet her. Working together they try to bribe her into having sex, threatening to say she has committed adultery if she refuses. When she refuses, the elders hold to the threat and make a public accusation of adultery. It is only after the two men are cross-examined by Daniel and reveal discrepancies in their stories that Suzanna is proven innocent.
Her pedestal depicts Biblical scenes. Suzanna's story is only considered to be canonical in the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches.In these denominations the story is part of the book of Daniel. In most other denominations of Christianity, Suzanna's story is not considered cannon, but it is considered to be useful for teaching. The motif of the story is very common in artwork. Images depicting the tale date back to as early as the 9th century. It was particularly popular in the 15th and 16th centuries. When painted the image usually depicts Suzanna and the two voyeurs in a scene. When sculpted in the round, Suzanna is usually depicted alone.
In the context of Krebs House, the Suzanna statue (KR23.2.27) sits atop the White Marble Pedestal (KR23.3.10), framed by a Italian Stone Rotunda (KR23.3.11), and set as the focal point of a fountain.

title: 1 of 2 Italian Statues (Hebe)
description:
Statue of a the Greek Goddess Hebe. She stands almost at Contrapposto, but looks more poised for movement, like she is about to step forward. In her right hand she holds a jug at her hip. The left holds a smaller dish, held at chest height, either for her to drink from or for her to pass. She wears a floor-length toga, that drapes from her left shoulder, leaving the right side of her chest bare. Her hair is pulled back, away from her face leaving her eyes visible where they look forward, past the cup, presumably to the viewer.
Hebe was primarily venerated as a goddess of eternal youth and the prime of life; Secondarily some groups also worship her as a goddess of forgiveness and mercy. She was the daughter of Zeus and Hera, divine wife of Hercules and the youngest of the Pantheon. Her primary role was as the cup bearer of the gods. This is related to her dominion over eternal youth and life, which she ensured by bearing ambrosia. She is sometimes depicted as an Eagle which bears a cup in it's talon instead of as a woman.
Her Roman counterpart is Juventas.
1 of 2 Italian statues that flank the back door. This one stands to the left side, when looking at the house from outside.

title: 2 of 2 Italian Marble Statues (Bather)
description:
A stone statue of a Venus bathing. She is bare except for a cloth draping over one hip, and held in her hands as if drying herself, or getting ready to get in the water. Her right side is supported by a stump, against which she leans, looking down toward her bare foot that steps off the edge of the pedestal. At the base of the stump, excess fabric from her draping is pooled, and a shell sits. Her hair is tied back, out of the way, and her eyes are cast down, but her face is peaceful.
The sculpture is a recreation of a marble sculpture by Etienne Maurice Falconet. The original is carved from marble and dates to 1757. The original title in French is "Baigneuse Entrer dans un bain." It is currently housed in the Louvre's Département des Sculptures du Moyen Age.

title: Diana Gabis (1 of 4 goddess statues)
description:
A depiction of the Roman goddess Diana. She stands dressed in sandals, and a tunic-style dress with flowing sleeves, She is positioned with two ends of a cloak in hand, reaching up to her right shoulder to fasten the clasp. Her hair is short and held in place by a band as she looks off to the left.
This statue is a recreation of a slightly larger marble sculpture depicting a young woman (probably the goddess Artemis or Diana) that is traditionally attributed to Praxiteles, a 4th Century BC sculptor from Greece. There are several known copies of the original statue, which has been lost to time. The most famous recreation is the Diana of Gabi which is on display at the Louvre in Paris. This version was acquired in 1807, and is featured as a part of the Bourghese Collection. The statue at the Louvre is slightly larger at 165 cm high.
